title: PKCS #1: RSA Cryptography Specifications Version 2.0
summary: Provides recommendations for implementing public-key cryptography based on the RSA algorithm, as the successor to RFC 2313. It covers encryption and signature schemes and their encodings. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 3447.

eli5.summary: RSA is a lock that anyone can close but only the owner can open. This document explains how to build and use that lock properly.

questions: how is rsa implemented in pkcs1 version 2.0
difference between oaep and pkcs1 v1.5
subtitle: How to use the RSA algorithm properly for encrypting keys and signing messages, including the new OAEP padding.

tldr.problem: Raw RSA math is not a usable encryption or signature system on its own. Implementations need agreed ways to turn messages into numbers, pad them, and write down keys and algorithm identifiers.
tldr.mechanism: PKCS #1 version 2.0 defines the RSA primitives, two encryption schemes (RSAES-OAEP and RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5), one signature scheme with appendix (RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5), their encoding methods, and ASN.1 syntax for keys and scheme identifiers.
tldr.outcome: It adds OAEP, the scheme recommended for new applications, while keeping the older PKCS #1 v1.5 methods for compatibility. This RFC was itself replaced by RFC 3447.

today: RFC 2437 is an Informational document that has been obsoleted by RFC 3447, so that is the specification to use. It replaced RFC 2313.

sections.title: What PKCS #1 Version 2.0 Covers
sections.content:
This memo is the successor to RFC 2313 and supersedes PKCS #1 version 1.5. It gives recommendations for implementing public-key cryptography based on the RSA algorithm, covering four things: cryptographic primitives, encryption schemes, signature schemes with appendix, and ASN.1 syntax for representing keys and identifying the schemes.

The recommendations are meant for general use, so they leave room for flexibility, and application standards built on them may add constraints. They are intended to be compatible with draft work in the ANSI X9F1 and IEEE P1363 groups. The editor's note says later versions may cover key size, key generation, key validation and signature schemes with message recovery.

The schemes only process data with a key. They do not cover obtaining or validating keys, so an application normally adds its own key management. The behavior of an implementation with an invalid key is unspecified.
sections.eli5: This is the rule book for using the RSA lock. It says how to build the lock and key and how to wrap a message before locking it. It leaves it to you to decide how to hand out the keys.

sections.title: Keys, Conversions and Primitives
sections.content:
An RSA public key is the pair (n, e): the modulus n, a product of two odd primes p and q, and the public exponent e. A private key is either the pair (n, d) or a quintuple (p, q, dP, dQ, qInv) that uses the Chinese Remainder Theorem to compute faster.

Two conversion primitives move between integers and octet strings: I2OSP (integer to octet string) and OS2IP (the reverse). The first octet is treated as the most significant.

The core primitives are plain exponentiation. RSAEP computes c = m^e mod n and RSADP undoes it with the private key. RSASP1 signs with the private key and RSAVP1 recovers the message representative with the public key. The RFC stresses that primitives are not meant to provide security apart from a scheme built on top of them.
sections.eli5: RSA is arithmetic on very large numbers. First the message is turned into a number, then a special power-and-remainder calculation scrambles it, and the secret key is the only thing that can unscramble it.

sections.title: The Two Encryption Schemes
sections.content:
An encryption scheme encodes the message, converts it to an integer, applies RSAEP and converts the result to a ciphertext of k octets, where k is the length of the modulus. A typical use is delivering a key confidentially, for example the content-encryption key in PKCS #7.

RSAES-OAEP is recommended for new applications. It handles messages up to k-2-2hLen octets, where hLen is the hash output length. With a suitable hash and large enough key it is described as plaintext-aware, so a chosen-ciphertext attack is ineffective against it. It also takes an encoding parameter string P, which may be empty.

RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 is the older scheme and is included only for compatibility, not recommended for new applications. It handles messages up to k-11 octets and is not plaintext-aware, so Bleichenbacher's chosen-ciphertext attack applies. The RFC lists countermeasures: add structure to the data, check conformance rigorously, and give only one kind of error message. It also advises generating the pseudorandom padding independently for each encryption, and notes the padding string is at least eight octets long. OAEP should not be mixed with PKCS1-v1_5 in one protocol.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to wrap a gift before locking it in the box. The newer wrapping, OAEP, is much harder to trick. The older wrapping is kept only so old programs still work.

sections.title: The Signature Scheme
sections.content:
The one signature scheme is RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, a signature scheme with appendix. To verify a signature you need the message itself, which is what separates it from schemes with message recovery, which are not supported here.

To sign, the message is hashed and encoded with EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5, converted to an integer, and signed with RSASP1. To verify, RSAVP1 recovers the encoded message, the verifier encodes the message again, and the two are compared. If they match the signature is valid.

The encoded message embeds a hash function identifier. As a result an attacker must break the particular hash function the signer chose, and attacking some other hash function is no use. The RFC mentions X.509 certificates as one use of such a signature. An editor's note says a PSS-based scheme is being investigated and would be recommended for new applications.
sections.eli5: To sign, you boil the message down to a short fingerprint, wrap it in a standard format and lock it with your private key. Anyone can check it by unlocking with your public key and comparing to their own fingerprint.

sections.title: Encoding Methods and Auxiliary Functions
sections.content:
Encoding methods turn octet-string messages into messages of the right length. EME-OAEP builds a data block DB = pHash || PS || 01 || M from a hash of the parameters, zero padding and the message. It then masks the block with a random seed using a mask generation function, and masks the seed in turn. EME-PKCS1-v1_5 builds EM = 02 || PS || 00 || M where PS is at least 8 nonzero pseudorandom octets. EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5 builds EM = 01 || PS || 00 || T where PS is FF bytes and T is the DER-encoded hash information.

Hash functions should be collision resistant. The RFC recommends MD2, MD5 and SHA-1, but for OAEP only SHA-1. For signatures SHA-1 is recommended for new applications, with MD2 and MD5 only for compatibility. MD4, allowed in version 1.5, is no longer allowed because of cryptanalytic progress. The mask generation function is MGF1, which builds a mask by hashing the seed together with a 4-octet counter.
sections.eli5: Before locking, the message is padded with extra filler and scrambled with a mixing recipe so that two identical messages do not look the same, and so a trickster cannot guess what is inside.

sections.title: ASN.1 Syntax for Keys and Schemes
sections.content:
Section 11 defines how to write keys and scheme names in ASN.1. A public key is an RSAPublicKey sequence of the modulus and the public exponent. A private key is an RSAPrivateKey sequence holding a version (0 for this document), the modulus, both exponents, the two primes, and the CRT values. The intended uses include X.509 certificates, PKCS #8 and PKCS #12.

Object identifiers name each scheme. rsaEncryption identifies keys and RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5. A separate identifier, id-RSAES-OAEP, carries parameters naming the hash function, the mask generation function and the encoding parameters, with SHA-1, MGF1 with SHA-1 and an empty string as defaults. RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 has one identifier for each of MD2, MD5 and SHA-1.

The memo also reproduces a patent statement for the RSA algorithm and a revision history that runs from versions 1.0 to 1.3 through to this version 2.0.
sections.eli5: This part is the labeling system. It says how to write a clear tag on each key and each lock, so the other person knows exactly which kind they are holding.
